title: I have a headache
title_target: ခေါင်း ကိုက်တယ် — hkowⁿ: kaik-tè
goal: Naming parts of the body and saying what hurts, then going to a pharmacy or clinic — including a few expressions of pain that can't be translated word for word from English.
bekal: naming the body parts people complain about most
telling apart နာတယ်, ကိုက်တယ်, and ဖျားတယ်
describing your symptoms to a doctor or pharmacist
asking after someone who is ill and wishing them well

dialogs.title: စကားပြော — At the pharmacy near the office
dialogs.intro: Ani has felt unwell since the morning and drops into a pharmacy. Watch for three words that English might all call "sick" or "hurt", but that never replace each other in Burmese.

grammars.title: ⚠️ Three words for "sick" that never replace each other
body: English already splits these up a little — "hurts", "aches", "has a fever" — and Burmese splits them strictly. Choosing the wrong one sounds as odd as saying "my head has a fever".

head: Word
Say it
Exact meaning
Example
rows: လည်ချောင်း နာတယ် — my throat hurts
ခေါင်း ကိုက်တယ် — I have a headache
ဖျားတယ် — I have a fever
နေမကောင်းဘူး

after: ⚠️ **ကိုက်တယ် literally means "to bite".** ခေါင်းကိုက်တယ် word for word is "head bites" — actually a very apt picture of a throbbing headache. It's used for the head, teeth, and muscles.
For a general complaint without pointing to a body part, နေမကောင်းဘူး is the safest and most common choice. If in doubt, start there and wait to be asked ဘယ်နား မကောင်းလဲ.

grammars.title: Saying which part hurts
body: The pattern is very simple: **body part + "hurt" verb**. No possessive, no "my" — if you're the one speaking, it's obvious whose body you mean.

head: Burmese
Say it
English
rows: ခေါင်း ကိုက်တယ်
ဗိုက် နာတယ်
သွား ကိုက်တယ်
လည်ချောင်း နာတယ်
ခါး နာတယ်
နှာ စေးတယ်
ဝမ်းသွားတယ်

after: ⚠️ Notice **သွား**, which here means "tooth", not "go". The two are written the same and both are said *thwa:* with high tone — so only the sentence tells them apart. Burmese has a few pairs like this, and context always rescues you.

grammars.title: How to take medicine
body: Frequency uses the pattern **time span + number + ကြိမ်** ("times"), and doses use the classifier that fits the form of the medicine.

head: Burmese
Say it
Meaning
rows: တစ်နေ့ သုံးကြိမ်
တစ်ကြိမ် တစ်လုံး

after: ⚠️ **မ…ခင် means "before"** and uses မ without ဘူး — the one place where မ appears without its partner. မစားခင် (before eating), မသွားခင် (before going), မိုးမကျခင် (before the rain comes), as in the dialogue in unit 14.

grammars.title: …ကတည်းက — since
body: To say since when something has been going on, use ကတည်းက (*ga.-dè:-ga.*) attached to the time word. The sentence almost always uses …နေတယ်, because the situation is still ongoing.

head: Burmese
Say it
Meaning
rows: မနေ့ကတည်းက
မနက်ကတည်းက
ငယ်ငယ်ကတည်းက
မနေ့ကတည်းက ကိုက်နေတယ်

after: To say for how long, use the time span plus ရှိပြီ: နှစ်ရက် ရှိပြီ (it's been two days). Put together: ခေါင်းကိုက်တာ နှစ်ရက် ရှိပြီ — "I've had a headache for two days".

sections.title: The body, medicine, and visiting the sick

blocks.text: Besides the body parts, there are a few sentences you'll need for visiting someone who is ill — and in Myanmar, visiting the sick is quite a serious social duty.

head: Burmese
Say it
Meaning
Burmese
Say it
Meaning
rows: လည်ချောင်း

head: Burmese
Say it
English
rows: ဆရာဝန် ပြတယ်
ဆေး သောက်တယ်
မြန်မြန် သက်သာပါစေ

blocks.title: Visiting the sick in Myanmar
items: **မြန်မြန် သက်သာပါစေ** (*myaⁿ-myaⁿ thèk-tha-ba-zay*) is a must-have sentence — "get well soon". The ending ပါစေ (*ba-zay*) makes a wish or blessing, and you've already met the same form in ကံကောင်းပါစေ (good luck).
Visiting the sick counts toward **ကုသိုလ်** (merit), so don't be surprised to find hospital rooms in Myanmar full of visitors. Bringing fruit is a safe custom.

⚠️ For serious health matters, don't rely on a pharmacy alone. Say ဆရာဝန် ပြချင်ပါတယ် ("I'd like to see a doctor") and ask for a referral. Many medicines in Myanmar are sold over the counter without a prescription, and that's no reason to diagnose yourself.
